brief: A stronger-than-expected preliminary September US PMI print pushed Treasury yields up more than 10bps intraday on Wednesday, with yields still two to three bps higher the next day. Before the release, most of the rise in longer-term yields had come from higher short-term rate expectations, while a yield-curve-derived term premium measure had been steadily falling since the Treasury's buyback announcement and the Fed's rate hike, cushioning the move. After the PMI, about half the rise in 30-year yields came from rising term premium, bond volatility jumped, and the curve steepened, which the author reads as the selloff turning more disorderly and carrying a higher risk premium. He argues stronger growth makes Treasuries riskier because it rests on a level of fiscal spending he calls wildly inappropriate for this stage of the cycle: cumulative deficits near $15 trillion since 2020 against unemployment averaging only 4.8%, which he says has turbocharged corporate profits funding AI infrastructure capex. He argues yields may not be done rising, since Treasuries are only back to their long-term mean and typically overshoot below it, and warns the selloff could become self-reinforcing as the 10-year nears 5.25%-5.50%, where Treasuries turn positively correlated with stocks and amplify rather than hedge portfolio losses.
